caseName: In re American Realty Capital Properties, Inc. Litigation (VEREIT/ARCP Securities Litigation)
court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York
keyFacts: American Realty Capital Properties Inc. (ARCP, later renamed VEREIT), a large publicly-traded net-lease REIT sponsored by Nicholas Schorsch's AR Capital/AR Global platform, misstated adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) by roughly $23 million in Q1-Q2 2014 to mask that it was missing an internal earnings metric. In October 2014 ARCP disclosed the errors, retracted 18 months of financial statements, and its CFO and chief accounting officer resigned; the stock fell more than 36%. The CAO (Lisa McAlister) pleaded guilty to securities fraud in 2016 and the CFO (Brian Block) was convicted at trial in 2017.
outcome: Settled on the eve of trial. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein granted final approval on January 21, 2020 to an aggregate $1.025 billion settlement fund, one of the largest securities class action recoveries ever against a REIT: VEREIT/ARCP itself contributed $738.5 million, the AR Capital/AR Global-affiliated manager entities and Schorsch-controlled parties contributed approximately $225-286.5 million (reported inconsistently across sources), former auditor Grant Thornton LLP paid $49 million, and former CFO Brian Block personally paid $12.5 million.
dollarAmountBasis: Aggregate approved class-action settlement fund across all settling defendants (issuer, external manager/sponsor entities, auditor, and individual CFO), as approved by the court on January 21, 2020.
notes: Cross-verified against Cohen Milstein's case summary (lead plaintiff's counsel), multiple contemporaneous news reports (InvestmentNews, Blue Vault, AltsWire, White Law Group), and the underlying VEREIT 8-K stipulations of settlement filed with the SEC (which could not be directly fetched due to a 403 response but are referenced consistently across secondary sources). This is the anchor 'mega-case' for the REIT securities-fraud claim type and sets the outer bound of realistic REIT securities exposure; most other cases in this dataset are one to three orders of magnitude smaller.

caseName: In re RAIT Financial Trust Securities Litigation
citation: Consolidated securities class action, E.D. Pa. (2009)
court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
keyFacts: RAIT Financial Trust, a commercial real estate finance REIT, was sued on behalf of purchasers of its securities between June 8, 2006 and August 3, 2007, alleging RAIT and certain executives violated Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5 by making material misrepresentations to the market about the company's financial condition and loan portfolio quality during that period.
outcome: The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania granted final approval on December 10, 2009 to a $32 million cash settlement, funded by RAIT's directors' and officers' liability insurers. The action was dismissed with prejudice and all defendants received a full release.
dollarAmountBasis: Total cash settlement fund, funded entirely by D&O insurance, per RAIT's own 8-K disclosure.
notes: Confirmed against RAIT's own SEC Form 8-K exhibit describing the settlement (found via search; underlying document not independently re-fetched but quoted consistently by StreetInsider and Bernstein Litowitz Berger & Grossmann, class counsel). Useful benchmark for a mid-size REIT (mortgage/commercial finance REIT, not equity REIT) 10b-5 case resolved entirely within insurance limits.

caseName: In re Luminent Mortgage Capital, Inc. Securities Litigation
court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of California
keyFacts: Luminent Mortgage Capital, Inc., a mortgage REIT, was charged with issuing materially false and misleading press releases and SEC filings regarding its financial results and business prospects during the run-up to the 2007-2008 mortgage/credit crisis, in violation of federal securities laws.
outcome: Judge Phyllis J. Hamilton preliminarily approved the settlement on January 20, 2009, and granted final approval on April 29, 2009 (also awarding class counsel 25% of the fund in fees), for an $8,000,000 all-cash settlement, with the action dismissed with prejudice.
dollarAmountBasis: Total cash settlement fund approved by the court.
notes: Sourced from a Stanford Securities Class Action Clearinghouse case page identified via web search; the Clearinghouse's own site (securities.stanford.edu) returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch during this research and displayed a banner indicating it is 'under construction' as of August 2026, so the underlying primary page could not be independently re-verified — hence 'medium' rather than 'high' confidence, even though Stanford SCAC is normally the strongest available source for this category. A small mortgage-REIT case, useful as a lower-bound data point for a distressed-credit-cycle REIT 10b-5 claim.

caseName: SEC v. W. P. Carey & Co. LLC, et al.
citation: SEC Litigation Release No. 20501; SEC Admin. Proc. File No. 3-13294 (2008-2009)
court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York / SEC administrative proceeding
keyFacts: W.P. Carey & Co., the external manager/sponsor of a family of non-traded REITs (the Corporate Property Associates, or 'CPA', series), paid nearly $10 million in undisclosed compensation between 2000 and 2003 to a broker-dealer that sold shares of the W.P. Carey REITs to retail investors, without disclosing those payments to the investors as required.
outcome: W.P. Carey settled the SEC's securities fraud charges by agreeing to pay approximately $30 million total (roughly $20 million in disgorgement and prejudgment interest plus a $10 million civil penalty). Two senior executives separately settled individual charges (one barred from serving as an officer/director for five years and paying a $240,000 penalty; the accountant suspended from practicing before the SEC for two years and paying a $75,000 penalty).
dollarAmountBasis: Total SEC settlement paid by W.P. Carey & Co. (disgorgement + prejudgment interest + civil penalty), excluding the separate smaller individual-defendant penalties.
notes: SEC enforcement action rather than a private class action, but directly on point for the 'REIT sponsor/advisor' fraud fact pattern in scope, with a real disclosed dollar figure from the regulator's own litigation release and administrative order (SEC Release No. 33-9051).

caseName: SEC v. United Development Funding III, L.P., United Development Funding IV, et al.
citation: SEC settled civil action; consent judgment entered July 2018, N.D. Tex.
court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of Texas
keyFacts: United Development Funding III and United Development Funding IV, non-traded mortgage REITs/funds investing in residential land development loans, failed to disclose that later investor capital was effectively being used to make distributions and pay off earlier investors and related entities as the funds ran into liquidity trouble, and used misleading marketing that touted annualized returns of up to 9.75% while the funds were losing money.
outcome: In July 2018, the entities and certain individuals consented to SEC judgments enjoining future securities-law violations and agreed to pay a combined $8.2 million in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. Separately and later, four top UDF executives (including CEO Hollis Greenlaw) were criminally convicted in January 2022 on multiple counts including securities fraud and conspiracy.
dollarAmountBasis: Combined disgorgement, interest, and civil penalties paid by the UDF entities and individuals under the 2018 SEC consent judgments (does not include any separate criminal restitution from the later 2022 convictions).
notes: Primary source is the SEC's own final judgment document. The subsequent criminal fraud convictions (2022) of the executives are a useful escalation data point showing how a REIT/fund-level SEC civil settlement can be followed by a much larger, separate criminal exposure for individuals — flag this dual-track pattern for the valuation tool if it ever models individual-defendant risk.

caseName: In re Inland Western Retail Real Estate Trust, Inc. Shareholder Litigation
citation: Shareholder derivative/class action, N.D. Ill. (filed Nov. 2007, settled 2010)
court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of Illinois
keyFacts: Inland Western Retail Real Estate Trust (a non-traded REIT then considering a stock exchange listing) agreed in 2007 to acquire four affiliated advisory and property-management firms from company insiders for $375 million in an all-stock deal, generating a large paper profit for those insiders. A pension fund shareholder sued in November 2007 alleging self-dealing and that the purchase price for the 'Internalization' had been inflated at the expense of public shareholders.
outcome: The parties reached a settlement that received preliminary court approval in July 2010: the insider sellers agreed to forfeit and return 9 million of the 37.5 million shares they had received in the internalization deal (valued at approximately $90 million at the time of the original transaction), and Inland Western separately agreed to cover up to $10 million of the plaintiffs' legal fees.
dollarAmountBasis: Value, at the time of the original 2007 transaction, of the 9 million shares the insider-sellers agreed to forfeit back to the company; does not include the additional up-to-$10 million in legal fees Inland Western separately agreed to pay.
notes: The remedy here was principally an in-kind stock forfeiture rather than a cash payment, so the $90 million figure is a valuation of returned consideration rather than a settlement check — flag this distinction in the valuation tool, since 'dollar value of relief' and 'cash paid' are not the same thing in self-dealing REIT internalization cases. Court identified as N.D. Ill. based on the reporting that the pension-fund plaintiff sued 'in U.S. District Court in Chicago'; exact docket number not independently confirmed.

caseName: Milliken v. American Realty Capital Hospitality Advisors, LLC, et al. (Hospitality Investors Trust Shareholder Derivative Litigation)
court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York
keyFacts: Shareholder derivative suit against the external advisor of Hospitality Investors Trust, Inc. (an AR Global-sponsored non-traded hotel REIT) and certain officers/directors, alleging breaches of fiduciary duty in connection with fee arrangements and related-party transactions between the REIT and its AR Global-affiliated manager.
outcome: On February 20, 2020, the court granted preliminary approval to a proposed settlement providing for an aggregate cash payment to the company of $15,181,108.47 (with $250,000 of that paid personally by the former CFO and the remainder by the company's D&O insurers), plus the tender of 83,504 shares of common stock back to the company. Final approval followed a June 9, 2020 settlement hearing, alongside a separate $2,250,000 award for plaintiff's counsel fees, expenses, and a case-contribution award. (Hospitality Investors Trust itself later filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2021, unrelated to this settlement.)
dollarAmountBasis: Aggregate cash payment to the company under the proposed derivative settlement, per the company's own SEC Form 8-K disclosure, excluding the separately awarded ~$2.25 million in plaintiff's-counsel fees/expenses and excluding the value of the 83,504 shares tendered back.
notes: Confirmed via the company's own 8-K filing and corroborated by Chimicles Schwartz Kriner & Donaldson-Smith (plaintiffs' counsel) and Blue Vault/AltsWire industry press. A good real-world data point for the size of a derivative-suit cash recovery (as opposed to a class-action recovery) against a REIT's external manager/officers over related-party fee conduct, distinct from a straight securities-fraud claim against the issuer itself.

caseName: Quinn v. Knight (Apple REIT Ten / Apple Hospitality REIT Derivative Litigation)
court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Virginia
keyFacts: Derivative suit brought by former Apple REIT Ten shareholder James Quinn alleging that Apple REIT Ten's 2016 merger into Apple Hospitality REIT was orchestrated by founder/executive chairman Glade Knight (who was also CEO and board chairman of Apple Ten) to benefit himself, his son, and other company insiders at the expense of REIT Ten's public shareholders, in breach of fiduciary duty.
outcome: The parties reached a settlement just days before trial; the court approved it on March 16, 2017, requiring Apple Hospitality REIT to pay $32 million to former Apple REIT Ten shareholders. Class counsel were awarded $8.96 million in fees (28% of the fund) plus roughly $430,000 in expense reimbursement, and the named plaintiff received a $15,000 incentive award. It was reported at the time as the largest derivative settlement in the Fourth Circuit.
dollarAmountBasis: Total cash settlement fund paid by Apple Hospitality REIT to former Apple REIT Ten shareholders, funded and paid in January 2017 per the company's own SEC disclosures.
notes: Court and case number confirmed via Justia docket (Quinn v. Knight et al., No. 3:2016cv00610, E.D. Va.). One of the largest disclosed non-traded-REIT merger self-dealing derivative recoveries in this dataset outside the ARCP/VEREIT mega-settlement, and a useful benchmark for 'founder/insider self-dealing in a REIT roll-up merger' fact patterns.

caseName: Moses v. Apple Hospitality REIT, Inc.
court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of New York
keyFacts: Class action filed April 22, 2014 on behalf of shareholders of Apple REIT Seven and Apple REIT Eight who purchased additional shares between July 17, 2007 and February 12, 2014 through the REITs' Dividend Reinvestment Plans (DRIP), alleging the DRIP purchase price was artificially inflated and did not reflect the true value of the units.
outcome: The parties reached an agreement in principle in January 2017 to settle for $5.5 million; the settlement was funded by the company in January 2018, and distribution of the net settlement fund to approved claimants occurred June 3, 2019.
dollarAmountBasis: Total cash settlement fund, per Apple Hospitality REIT's own SEC filings and the Leagle.com court decision record.
notes: A useful example of a non-traded-REIT DRIP/valuation-based 10b-5-adjacent claim (overstated NAV used to price reinvested-dividend share purchases) as distinct from a conventional 'stock price dropped after a restatement' fact pattern.

caseName: In re Wells Real Estate Investment Trust, Inc. Securities Litigation (Piedmont Office Realty Trust)
court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of Georgia
keyFacts: Wells Real Estate Investment Trust (later renamed Piedmont Office Realty Trust) filed a proxy statement on February 26, 2007 soliciting shareholder approval to internalize management by merging its external advisor affiliates into the REIT for $175 million worth of company stock. Two consolidated class actions alleged the proxy statement contained materially misleading disclosures about the internalization and that the transaction breached fiduciary duties owed to shareholders.
outcome: Piedmont announced on October 22, 2012 that it had reached agreements in principle to settle both consolidated class actions for a combined $7.5 million ($4.9 million and $2.6 million respectively), resolving the litigation and related appeals following court approval.
dollarAmountBasis: Combined total of the two agreed-in-principle settlement amounts ($4,900,000 + $2,600,000) disclosed in Piedmont's own SEC Form 8-K press release.
notes: Directly on point for the 'proxy disclosure claim' bucket in the internalization-vote context (structurally similar to the liquidity-event/charter-amendment votes at issue in the Lightstone REIT matter already tracked on the site), with a real, disclosed, non-trivial dollar settlement — useful as a mid-size proxy-disclosure benchmark rather than the all-or-nothing 'dismissed with no damages' outcomes seen in some other proxy cases in this dataset (e.g., St. Clair-Hibbard, below).

caseName: Cole Credit Property Trust III, Inc. Shareholder Litigation
citation: Circuit Court for Baltimore City, Maryland (consolidated, filed March 2013)
court: Circuit Court for Baltimore City, Maryland
keyFacts: A Cole Credit Property Trust III, Inc. shareholder sued in March 2013 seeking to block the REIT's proposed takeover/internalization combining Cole Credit Property Trust III with Cole Holdings Corporation to form Cole Real Estate Investments, Inc., alleging the transaction and related consolidated 'Cole Holdings Action' involved inadequate process and disclosure.
outcome: The court dismissed the case with prejudice on October 22, 2013. Plaintiffs appealed; the appeal was itself dismissed on July 31, 2014, but as part of that resolution the defendants agreed to reimburse plaintiffs' counsel in the consolidated Cole Holdings Action $100,000.
dollarAmountBasis: Fee/expense reimbursement paid to plaintiffs' counsel upon dismissal of the appeal — not a damages recovery or transaction-price adjustment.
notes: A useful counterexample: most REIT merger-objection suits do not win a real damages recovery, and this one resulted in outright dismissal with only a nominal fee payment to make the appeal go away — illustrative of the low real-dollar yield of the median merger-objection claim absent a strong self-dealing angle (contrast with Quinn v. Knight above, where a similar-sounding claim type recovered $32 million because it reached a derivative breach-of-duty theory rather than a pure disclosure theory).

caseName: Katz v. CommonWealth REIT; Central Laborers' Pension Fund v. CommonWealth REIT (Equity Commonwealth Trustee Litigation)
citation: Circuit Court for Baltimore City, Maryland (Katz Action, filed March 2013; Central Laborers Action, filed April 2013)
court: Circuit Court for Baltimore City, Maryland
keyFacts: Two shareholder suits against CommonWealth REIT (an externally-managed office/industrial REIT managed by RMR, later renamed Equity Commonwealth after activist investors Corvex and Related won a 2014 vote to replace the entire board) alleged the former trustees breached fiduciary duties, were unjustly enriched, and wasted corporate assets in connection with the RMR management arrangement and related governance practices.
outcome: Equity Commonwealth (the REIT's new name/management following the 2014 board overhaul) entered into a Settlement and Release Agreement on July 31, 2015 resolving both actions. The settlement was overwhelmingly non-monetary — largely mooted by the 2014 change in control and governance reforms already implemented — with the company agreeing to pay $200,000 toward plaintiffs' counsel's costs and expenses.
dollarAmountBasis: Cost/expense reimbursement paid to plaintiffs' counsel under the settlement agreement, per Equity Commonwealth's own SEC Form 8-K; no separate damages fund was paid because the underlying governance change (a full board replacement via proxy contest) had already occurred before settlement.
notes: Illustrates a distinct settlement pattern for REIT fiduciary-duty derivative suits: where an activist-investor proxy contest already achieves the practical remedy (removing the offending board), the follow-on derivative litigation tends to resolve for a small fee payment rather than a real damages recovery, because the 'real' relief already happened outside the courtroom.

caseName: St. Clair-Hibbard v. American Finance Trust, Inc., et al.
court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York (affirmed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit)
keyFacts: A shareholder of American Finance Trust, Inc. (AFIN), a non-traded REIT sponsored by AR Global, alleged that the proxy materials AFIN issued in late 2016/early 2017 soliciting stockholder approval of both a merger and an internalization advisory agreement were materially incomplete and misleading — allegedly omitting the risk that the REIT would trade at a discount once internalized and listed. Claims included violations of Exchange Act Sections 14(a), 20(a), and 20(b), plus breach of fiduciary duty against the external advisor, allegedly aided and abetted by AR Global and its principals.
outcome: The district court (Judge Lorna G. Schofield) dismissed the second amended complaint for failure to state a claim on September 23, 2019, holding the proxy disclosures were not materially misleading because AFIN had adequately warned of internalization-related conflicts and discount-trading risk, and industry-wide skepticism of externally-managed REITs was already public knowledge. The Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal in 2020.
notes: Kept despite the absence of a dollar figure because it establishes load-bearing doctrine for the proxy_disclosure_claim bucket: the Second Circuit's materiality analysis (adequate disclosure of conflict-of-interest and trading-discount risk defeats a proxy claim even without quantifying the risk) directly informs how strong a non-traded REIT's proxy-disclosure defense is likely to be, and stands in useful contrast to the Lightstone REIT proxy case (below), where a materially similar-sounding claim survived a motion to dismiss because the proxy allegedly concealed a specific insider's undisclosed financial stake rather than a generic industry-wide risk.

caseName: In re Lightstone REIT Proxy Litigation (Lightstone Value Plus REIT I, II, and III)
court: U.S. District Court, District of New Jersey
keyFacts: Putative class action against three affiliated non-traded Lightstone REITs, their external advisers, and individual directors, alleging that 2022 proxy statements soliciting shareholder approval of charter amendments eliminating scheduled liquidation deadlines concealed chairman David Lichtenstein's conflicting financial stake — subordinated participation interests allegedly worth over $59.8 million that would have been worthless had the REITs liquidated on schedule — and that phone solicitors misleadingly told undecided shareholders a 'yes' vote was the path to liquidity when it actually eliminated the liquidation deadline.
outcome: U.S. District Judge Michael A. Shipp denied the defendants' motion to dismiss on August 5, 2026, finding the proxy materials may have omitted the material conflict of interest and allowing all four counts (including breach of fiduciary duty) to proceed into discovery. No settlement or trial outcome yet; case is ongoing as of this research.
notes: Already tracked on the CREdocket site (id live-XXX in js/data.js) as a pending matter; included here as the anchor proxy_disclosure_claim case for this research batch because the task specifically flagged it as a starting point. No dollar outcome exists yet since the case survived only a motion to dismiss; the $59.8 million figure in the facts is the alleged value of the concealed conflicting interest, not a damages or settlement figure, and should not be used as a dollarAmount.

caseName: Blackwells Capital LLC v. Global Net Lease, Inc. and The Necessity Retail REIT, Inc.
citation: Circuit Court for Baltimore City, Maryland, and related S.D.N.Y. action (filed Dec. 2022)
court: Circuit Court for Baltimore City, Maryland / U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York
keyFacts: Activist investor Blackwells Capital sued Global Net Lease, Inc. and The Necessity Retail REIT, Inc. (both AR Global-managed REITs) in a proxy fight, alleging AR Global had extracted approximately $838 million in management fees from the two REITs — roughly four times the industry-standard fee level — through self-dealing management contracts approved by conflicted boards.
outcome: In June 2023, Global Net Lease, Necessity Retail REIT, their advisors/property managers, and AR Global entered into a cooperation agreement with Blackwells Capital: all parties released claims predating the settlement and dismissed the Maryland state and New York federal actions, Blackwells withdrew its board nominations, and Blackwells agreed to vote in favor of the REITs' subsequent merger and internalization transactions. No cash payment to the REITs or their shareholders was disclosed as part of the settlement.
notes: The $838 million figure is the alleged cumulative management-fee extraction over time, not a settlement or judgment amount — the litigation itself resolved via a governance/voting cooperation agreement with no disclosed cash component, which is a common outcome pattern for activist-driven self-dealing suits against externally-managed REITs (the practical leverage comes from the parallel proxy fight, not the lawsuit's damages theory).

caseName: In re Government Properties Income Trust / Select Income REIT Merger Litigation (Chen v. Select Income REIT; Schwartz v. Select Income REIT; Sinkula v. Select Income REIT; Scarantino v. Fraiche)
citation: Four parallel actions: S.D.N.Y. (filed Nov. 9 & 19, 2018), D. Mass. (filed Nov. 15, 2018), and Circuit Court for Baltimore City, MD (filed Nov. 16, 2018)
court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York; U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts; Circuit Court for Baltimore City, Maryland
keyFacts: Government Properties Income Trust and Select Income REIT (both managed by The RMR Group) announced a September 17, 2018 merger agreement to combine into what became Office Properties Income Trust. Four separate shareholder suits, filed within roughly a week of each other in three different courts, alleged the joint proxy statement/prospectus for the shareholder vote on the merger omitted material information, in violation of proxy-disclosure obligations.
outcome: The merger closed; the parallel disclosure suits followed the common 'disclosure-only' resolution pattern for merger-objection suits — the companies filed supplemental proxy disclosures addressing the alleged omissions (visible in the SEC Form S-4/A amendments filed shortly before the shareholder vote), after which the suits were mooted/withdrawn. No separate cash settlement fund to shareholders was disclosed.
notes: Textbook example of the 'multi-forum disclosure-only merger objection' pattern that is extremely common in REIT M&A: near-simultaneous duplicate suits in several courts, resolved by supplemental proxy disclosure rather than any damages payment (federal courts, following the Delaware Trulia decision and similar rulings, have grown increasingly skeptical of awarding plaintiffs' counsel a 'mootness fee' for this kind of resolution, per the 2022 In re: contemporaneous D&O Diary commentary), so this case type should generally be modeled in the valuation tool as low-dollar-value litigation risk even though it is filed frequently.
